YOUR SECTOR • Makers' Quarter

Meet Makers' Quarter

Know the themes. Meet the people. Explore several everyday situations.

Creator rights, credit, plagiarism and AI

Handle artwork, music, schoolwork and AI assistance. Find a way to create something good while treating other creators fairly.

Permission and licences

Permission says what use is allowed. A licence sets reuse conditions. Being online does not mean “free to use however I like”.

Credit and plagiarism

Credit identifies the creator and source. Presenting someone else’s work or ideas as your own is plagiarism. Credit does not replace permission.

Honest AI use

Explain what you made and what a tool helped with. Follow the task’s rules and check the output.

Mina

Creates characters and posters. Wants her name attached and her choices respected.

Jay

Good at editing quickly. A deadline can tempt him to skip the permission check.

By the end, you will be able to:
  • Distinguish permission from credit
  • Read reuse conditions
  • Describe your contribution honestly

Use the fictional details given. You never need to share a personal incident.

The reuse desk

Read the reuse cards, then decide.

Apply conditions: Use the stated terms instead of guessing what the creator would probably allow.

ART CARD

Mina’s mascot

“Use on the school noticeboard poster only.” Jay wants it on stickers sold through a public page.

MUSIC CARD

Beat by Ellis

A search result

THINK DEEPER • Makers' Quarter

Repair the credit

Use clues, consider perspectives and test your judgement.

→
Repair a misleading caption.

Construct an honest credit: Identify the creator, source and your contribution so the audience can understand what you made.

FICTIONAL SCREEN
Club design page
Jay’s published caption

“My original character. Took me ages.”

Project record

Mina made “Night Market Fox”. It came from her class portfolio. She agreed to use in this school slideshow with credit. Jay changed the background only.

Identify the title, creator and source.

State what Jay changed. Do not claim he drew the character.

Make the limit of this permission clear.

Repaired caption

Your credit will assemble here.

A good credit is accurate, not impressive-sounding. Changing a background does not make the original character yours.

TAKE ACTION • Makers' Quarter

Deadline decisions

Turn your understanding into a practical response.

→
Choose a practical next step in each event.

Decide under pressure: Keep the goal, but change a route that depends on misleading claims or missing permission.

1 · The sticker order closes at 4. Mina can only review the proof after school. What should the club do?

2 · AI rewrites most of Ellis’s assessment paragraph. The task permits ideas, but the submitted explanation must be his own. What now?

Choose one event above. Explain an effect on the creator, audience or teacher beyond “getting into trouble”.

STRETCH • Makers' Quarter

A remix with strings attached

Take the optional Ethical Creator challenge route.

Optional challenge · explain the tension, then defend a practical response.

THE REMIX BRIEF

Two permissions, one video

Mina allows her character in a school video but says no changes to the character. Ellis allows his music with credit. Jay wants an AI tool to animate Mina’s character and mix the music into a public advert for a local business.

Identify TWO parts of the plan that need checking. Say who must be asked and what you would ask.

Suggest a version the team could begin while waiting for replies.

Two checks before publishing

Lock in the key idea and prepare to save.

Explain what credit tells an audience.

Explain what permission tells the user of the work.

Key terms

Permission and licencesPermission says what use is allowed. A licence sets reuse conditions. Being online does not mean “free to use however I like”.
Credit and plagiarismCredit identifies the creator and source. Presenting someone else’s work or ideas as your own is plagiarism. Credit does not replace permission.
Honest AI useExplain what you made and what a tool helped with. Follow the task’s rules and check the output.
CopyrightLegal protection for original creative work.
AttributionNaming the creator and source clearly.
PermissionAgreement from the rights holder to use something in a particular way.
PlagiarismPresenting someone else’s work or ideas as your own.
LicenceRules explaining how work may be used, changed or shared.
RemixA new work made by combining or adapting existing material.
